title: The Embryo and the Funeral: Rosenblatt's Perceptron, the Press That Celebrated It, and the Book That Buried It
search_title: Rosenblatt's Perceptron: the 1958 press and Minsky and Papert's 1969 book
description: In July 1958 the US Navy unveiled a machine its creator said was 'the first machine which is capable of having an original idea.' The claim was Rosenblatt's, the headline was the New York Times's, and the reckoning came eleven years later when Minsky and Papert published a book of rigorous mathematics that the field read, wrongly, as a death certificate. This essay tells the story of how a genuine breakthrough became entangled with hype, how the critique that followed was at once correct and catastrophically misunderstood, and why the whole episode looks, from 2026, uncomfortably familiar.
standfirst: Frank Rosenblatt told the Navy his machine would one day be conscious. Marvin Minsky had once built the same kind of machine. What happened next took a quarter-century and more to undo.
body:
## The Press Conference In July 1958, the United States Office of Naval Research unveiled what it called "the first machine which is capable of having an original idea," in the words of its creator, Frank Rosenblatt.1 In objective terms, the machine had done something modest: after fifty trials with a deck of punch cards, an IBM 704, a five-ton computer, had taught itself to tell cards marked on the left from cards marked on the right. Rosenblatt was a research psychologist of twenty-nine, and he did not describe what had happened in modest terms. The perceptron was not a fraud, and Rosenblatt was not a fool. But before the week was out, his invention had been assigned a future it could not yet earn, and the gap between the machine and the promise would take a quarter-century and more to close. Rosenblatt had written: "Stories about the creation of machines having human qualities have long been a fascinating province in the realm of science fiction. Yet we are about to witness the birth of such a machine – a machine capable of perceiving, recognizing and identifying its surroundings without any human training or control."2 The next morning, the New York Times published a report under the headline: "NEW NAVY DEVICE LEARNS BY DOING: Psychologist Shows Embryo of Computer Designed to Read and Grow Wiser."3 Based on Rosenblatt's statements at the press conference, the Times reported the perceptron as "the embryo of an electronic computer that [the Navy] expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence."4 In late November, the New Yorker weighed in: "Indeed, it strikes us as the first serious rival to the human brain ever devised."5 This was a great deal to claim for a machine that had learned to sort punch cards. To understand what happened next, the excitement, the backlash, the years of stagnation, and the eventual vindication, it helps to begin earlier, with the ideas Rosenblatt had inherited and the problem he was genuinely trying to solve. ## The Lineage The story of the perceptron begins, as so much in early AI does, with a 1943 paper by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts. McCulloch was a neurophysiologist. Pitts was something stranger: he left home in Detroit at fifteen to study and went to Chicago.6 At the University of Chicago he sat in on Bertrand Russell's lectures without registering as a student. Russell was visiting Chicago in the fall of 1938, and he directed Pitts to go study with the logician Rudolf Carnap.7 Pitts duly obtained a copy of Carnap's book *The Logical Syntax of Language*, read it, walked into Carnap's office during office hours with the book filled with corrections and suggested improvements, and then disappeared. Almost a year went by before Carnap was able to contact him again and help him secure a student job.8 McCulloch later invited Pitts and his friend Jerome Lettvin to live with his family; the evening collaboration between McCulloch and Pitts produced the paper that would follow. Together they published "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity" in the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, proposing the first mathematical model of the nervous system as a network of simple logical elements.9 Their artificial neurons received inputs, performed a weighted sum, and fired an output signal based on a threshold function; by connecting them in various configurations, McCulloch and Pitts showed their model could perform all logical functions.10 The brain, they argued, was in some sense a digital computer, and a digital computer could therefore model the brain. This was electrifying and, in large part, correct. Six years later, Donald Hebb, a psychologist at McGill University, published *The Organization of Behavior* (1949), proposing a rule for how synapses learn. The connection between two neurons is strengthened when one repeatedly and persistently takes part in firing the other.11 The phrase later distilled from this, "cells that fire together, wire together," was not Hebb's own, but the idea was, and it supplied the engineering intuition that Rosenblatt would translate into mathematics. The McCulloch-Pitts neuron was clever but rigid: its connections were fixed. What Rosenblatt added was the ability to learn. He introduced modifiable, continuously valued weights between units. The key innovation was the learning rule: modifiable weights that adjusted in response to error, absent from the fixed McCulloch-Pitts model.12 Marvin Minsky, who would later become Rosenblatt's most formidable critic, had in 1951 built one of the first hardware neural networks, a machine called SNARC, the Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator. Minsky was then a graduate student in mathematics at Princeton; his collaborator Dean Edmonds was a physics graduate student there who volunteered that he was good with electronics.13 SNARC comprised roughly forty Hebb synapses and modelled a rat running a maze, built partly from the surplus autopilot of a B-24 bomber.14 That the man who built one of the first hardware neural networks would later write the book credited with ending neural network research for a generation is one of the odder ironies in the history of computing. The world into which Rosenblatt's perceptron arrived in 1958 was not empty. The Dartmouth workshop of 1956 had given the field its name and its founding ambitions: Newell and Simon arrived there with a working program, the Logic Theorist, that could prove theorems from *Principia Mathematica* by manipulating symbols according to formal rules, the demonstration that would define symbolic AI as a research programme.15 McCarthy, Minsky, Newell, and Simon were already working on programs that manipulated logical symbols rather than adjusting numerical weights. Their approach competed for the same limited federal funds. One figure whose position mattered enormously was J. C. R. Licklider, head of the Information Processing Techniques Office at ARPA, the main federal funder of AI research. Licklider had been interested in biologically inspired and self-organizing methods in the 1950s, but by the mid-1960s he was openly critical of them, including the perceptron, and strongly favoured the logical AI approach of Simon and Newell instead.16 The dispute between connectionist and symbolic AI was never purely a matter of mathematics. It was also a matter of money and of which style of work the primary funder believed in. Rosenblatt was not the only person developing a learning network in this period. At Stanford in 1960, Bernard Widrow and his doctoral student Marcian Hoff developed ADALINE, the Adaptive Linear Neuron, a single-layer network trained by the least mean squares algorithm, which minimised the squared error on every training example rather than responding only to outright misclassification.17 ADALINE found commercial application in adaptive noise filtering and telephone switching; MADALINE, the multilayer version, was demonstrated on tasks including weather forecasting and speech recognition.18 Connectionism in 1958 was already a research programme with multiple contributors, not a single eccentric's hobby. ## The Boy from New Rochelle Frank Rosenblatt was born in New Rochelle, New York, on 11 July 1928, the son of Dr. Frank Rosenblatt.19 He attended the Bronx High School of Science, the same school Minsky attended, though Minsky was a grade behind him, before going to Cornell, where he took his undergraduate degree in social psychology in 1950 and his doctorate in 1956.20 Even his dissertation showed what kind of mind he had: he built a custom computer, the Electronic Profile Analyzing Computer, to run multidimensional analysis on psychometric data from more than two hundred Cornell undergraduates; fifteen minutes of data processing took just two seconds.21 After his doctorate he moved to the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York, where he worked successively as a research psychologist, senior psychologist, and eventually head of the cognitive systems section.22 It was there, beginning in 1957, that he developed the perceptron. His first technical report, titled "The Perceptron: A Perceiving and Recognizing Automaton," appeared in January 1957 as a Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory report under Project PARA; the landmark journal paper, "The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain," was published in *Psychological Review* in 1958.23 The title is telling. He was not, in his own mind, building a machine. He was doing psychology. The perceptron was a model of the brain, a hypothesis about how biological neural systems might actually store and retrieve information. His conception of the device had three layers. An array of sensory units detected the input. A hidden layer of association units processed signals from the sensory layer along connections that were set randomly at the outset: randomly, because Rosenblatt believed the retina was itself randomly connected to the visual cortex, and he wanted his machine to resemble human visual perception.24 The association units then fed response units whose weighted connections were the ones that actually learned: encoded in potentiometers, with weight updates performed by small electric motors.25 His 1958 paper opened with three questions about the brain's information-processing capabilities: how does it sense the physical world, in what form is information stored in memory, and how does information in memory influence recognition and behavior?26 These are still the right questions. The full scope of what Rosenblatt actually proved is easily lost in accounts that concentrate on the 1958 press conference and the 1969 rebuttal. His 1962 book *Principles of Neurodynamics* is the primary technical document of record. It proved that an elementary perceptron with an unlimited number of hidden-layer units could solve any classification problem, an existence theorem of genuine mathematical force.27 The book also studied what it called cross-coupled perceptrons, machines with connections between units in the same layer, which are now recognised as precursors to Hopfield networks; back-coupled networks, with connections from later layers to earlier ones; four-layer perceptrons in which the last two layers had adjustable weights; and networks incorporating time delays for processing sequential data.28 The Minsky-Papert book published seven years later would address a far simpler subclass of machines than this. ## The Hype Machine The July 1958 press conference was arranged by the Office of Naval Research, which had funded the work. The Navy had its own reasons to emphasise the promise of a learning machine during the Cold War, and Rosenblatt had a temperamental preference for the large claim over the cautious one. His former doctoral student George Nagy later said: "On a scale of 1 to 10, he would have rated its significance 10."29 What is interesting, looking back, is how rational the excitement was at the level of the idea even if not at the level of the machine. The convergence theorem, proved by Rosenblatt, with Block providing a contemporaneous independent proof and Novikoff a third clean proof in 1962, showed that if a classification problem could in principle be solved by a perceptron's architecture, then the learning algorithm would converge on a solution in a finite number of steps.30 This was a mathematically solid guarantee of learning. If the brain used something like a perceptron, and if the human brain could learn anything at all, then perhaps the perceptron could too. The leap from theorem to prediction was large, but it was not delusional. It was the kind of extrapolation that every field makes at the moment a new tool first arrives. By 1959, Rosenblatt had moved to Cornell's main campus in Ithaca as director of the Cognitive Systems Research Program.31 The Mark I Perceptron had an input retina of four hundred photocells arranged in a twenty-by-twenty grid, a hidden layer of 512 association units, and eight response units.32 It was designed for image classification. The CIA's Photo Division studied the Mark I from 1960 to 1964 for the recognition of militarily interesting silhouetted targets, planes and ships, in aerial photographs; separately, a four-year programme at the National Photographic Interpretation Center ran from 1963 through 1966 to develop the algorithm into a working tool for photo-interpreters.33 Rosenblatt's laboratory culture was extraordinary. He recruited a sixteen-year-old Cornell freshman named Terrell Koken over a conversation about Fermat's Last Theorem in the music lounge, bought a $3,000 telescope and a house in Brooktondale to put it in, and his graduate students built an observatory in the pasture at night.34 His follow-up to the Mark I, the Tobermory, named after the talking cat in an H. H. Munro story, was designed for speech recognition, had four layers and 12,000 weights implemented in toroidal magnetic cores, occupied an entire room, and was built between 1961 and 1967.35 By then, the world had changed. Rosenblatt called Minsky "the loyal opposition."36 They had known each other since school; at conferences, Rosenblatt and Minsky publicly debated the perceptron's viability as their colleagues and students looked on in amazement. "Rosenblatt had a vision that he could make computers see and understand language," Thorsten Joachims, a machine learning professor at Cornell, has said. "And Marvin Minsky pointed out that that's not going to happen, because the functions are just too simple."37 ## The Loyal Opposition Writes a Book When Seymour Papert arrived at MIT in 1963, he and Minsky decided to write a systematic mathematical account of the limitations of perceptrons.38 Papert brought a specific kind of mathematical training to the project. He held two doctoral degrees: the first from the University of the Witwatersrand in 1952, the second from the University of Cambridge in 1959, with a thesis on the lattices of logic and topology; he had also spent several years at the University of Geneva working with Jean Piaget on how children learn mathematics.39 It was Papert's topological and geometric apparatus that gave the critique of the perceptron the formal depth that Minsky's earlier informal objections had lacked. It took them until 1969 to finish, not because the project was simple but because mathematical problems kept unexpectedly requiring resolution as they wrote.40 Before the book appeared, an unpublished technical manuscript had already circulated in the field and was used, by some accounts, to redirect funding away from neural network research toward symbolic AI.41 *Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry*, published by MIT Press in 1969, is a work of genuine mathematical elegance.42 Its central results concern parity and connectedness. Minsky and Papert took as their subject abstract versions of a class of learning devices, called perceptrons, "in recognition of the pioneer work of Frank Rosenblatt."43 These were single-layer machines in which each unit received connections from only a small part of the input, what the authors called conjunctive localness. Under this restriction, Minsky and Papert proved that a single-layer perceptron cannot compute the parity function without the order of connections growing without bound as the input grows, and cannot reliably determine whether a figure in the input retina is connected without connections growing at least as fast as the square root of the input size.44 These are genuine mathematical results. The book was dedicated to Rosenblatt. H. D. Block, who had independently proved the convergence theorem contemporaneously with Rosenblatt's own work, was better placed than almost anyone to identify what Minsky and Papert had ignored. His 1970 review argued that they had chosen to study "a severely limited class of machines from a viewpoint quite alien to Rosenblatt's," and that the title of the book was "seriously misleading."45 Block's objection had a precise technical basis: *Principles of Neurodynamics* had proved that an unrestricted elementary perceptron with sufficiently many hidden-layer units can solve any classification problem; it had studied four-layer networks, back-coupled networks, and cross-coupled networks now known as Hopfield networks. Minsky and Papert had taken the simplified, single-layer, conjunctively local perceptron and written a book about it. The results were correct. The subject was narrow. The field treated the former as establishing the latter. Bernard Widrow said Minsky and Papert's proofs were "pretty much irrelevant," coming a full decade after Rosenblatt's perceptron.46 Allen Newell, reviewing the book for *Science*, called it "a great book."47 ## The Problem With the Problem In a 1971 Progress Report circulated to funding agencies under Minsky and Papert's names, they wrote of what they called Gamba perceptrons, two-layer machines in which the first layer is also made of linear threshold units rather than boolean units, that "virtually nothing is known about the computational capabilities of this latter kind of machine. We believe that it can do little more than can a low order perceptron."48 This claim was directed at funders at a moment when funding decisions were being made. It was also wrong. Mikel Olazaran's sociological study of the perceptrons controversy, published in *Social Studies of Science* in 1996, identifies two distinct modes in the reception of the book. Specialists who read it carefully understood the precise technical content and its limits. A broader community treated the book as having demonstrated a comprehensive refutation of the entire connectionist enterprise, what Olazaran characterised as the book's official history.49 This official reading was promoted by researchers in symbolic AI who believed neural network funding was being diverted from their projects, and it became the version taught and cited for a generation. Minsky himself later compared *Perceptrons* to the Necronomicon in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction: "often cited but never read."50 When the 1988 expanded edition of *Perceptrons* appeared, Minsky and Papert had a second opportunity, after nearly twenty years, to correct the misreading their book had suffered. They did not take it. The prologue and epilogue added to that edition engaged with the 1980s neural network revival, but Minsky and Papert largely doubled down: they conjectured that multilayer nets were a "sterile" extension and that Gamba machines would require "an enormous number" of Gamba-masks.51 The 1988 edition is the strongest evidence in the whole episode that the pessimism was not merely a misreading by others but a position Minsky and Papert actively maintained even as experiments were refuting it. These conjectures were wrong. The algorithm that would prove them wrong had been sitting in a Harvard doctoral dissertation since 1974. Paul Werbos had described backpropagation, the technique of training multilayer networks by propagating error signals backward through the layers, as part of his thesis, well before the field took notice.52 Rumelhart had developed it independently in spring 1982; when he, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published their landmark paper in *Nature* in 1986, they claimed to have overcome the problems Minsky and Papert had identified, that "their pessimism about learning in multilayer machines was misplaced."53 ## The End and the Aftermath Rosenblatt did not live to see the consequences of *Perceptrons* fully unfold. He died on 11 July 1971, his forty-third birthday, in a boating accident in Chesapeake Bay.54 He was eulogised on the floor of the House of Representatives by, among others, former Senator Eugene McCarthy, for whose 1968 presidential campaign Rosenblatt had worked in New Hampshire and California.55 When he died, his research had moved far from the perceptron: from 1966 onward he had been studying whether learned behaviour could be transferred from trained to untrained rats by the injection of brain extracts, and he published extensively in this area in his final years.56 It was the kind of outsize, risky question that defined his career. Richard O'Brien, former director of Cornell's Division of Biological Sciences, said at Rosenblatt's memorial service: "He would never, as prudent professors do, pick out some small aspect of the physical universe which could be studied and could reasonably be expected to produce solutions in a year or two. Instead, he would reach out and grasp the biggest problems that he could see, and apply himself, throw himself into the study of them, without any recognition of the fact that if he made bad choices, or if he chose, as he usually did, problems which were not likely to yield a solution within 10 or 20 years, that this would redound to his disadvantage. He never worked that way."57 Minsky received the ACM Turing Award for 1969, computing's highest honour, presented the following year.58 Neural network research did not entirely disappear in the 1970s. A few researchers, James Anderson, Teuvo Kohonen, Stephen Grossberg, continued to work on connectionist systems, though they were very much the exception rather than the rule.59 The AI funding that had been flowing toward perceptrons moved to symbolic AI. It is worth being precise about what happened next, since two different stories are easily conflated. The decline of neural network research in the decade after 1969 was attributable in part to *Perceptrons* and in part to Licklider's prior turn against biologically inspired methods at IPTO. The broader AI winter of the mid-1970s and early 1980s was a separate event: it came from the failure of symbolic AI's own promises, documented in the Lighthill Report of 1973 and in successive DARPA reviews. These were the consequences of different bets going wrong at different times. The revival when it came had two distinct lines. In 1982, John Hopfield published a paper on content-addressable memory: he showed that a recurrent network of simple threshold units would settle into stable states that could store and retrieve patterns, and he described this behaviour using an energy function borrowed from statistical physics.60 Separately, Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams made backpropagation practical for multilayer feedforward networks in their 1986 *Nature* paper.61 Then in 1989, Yann LeCun and colleagues at AT&T Bell Laboratories published a paper in *Neural Computation* demonstrating backpropagation applied to a convolutional network for recognising handwritten zip-code digits, the direct heir, in vision terms, to what Rosenblatt had been trying to do with the Mark I Perceptron three decades earlier.62 The Mark I Perceptron now resides in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, DC. The IEEE established the Frank Rosenblatt Award in 2004.63 "What Rosenblatt wanted," Joachims has said, "was to show the machine objects and have it recognize those objects. And 60 years later, that's what we're finally able to do. So he was heading on the right track, he just needed to do it a million times over."64 ## What to Make of It Frank Rosenblatt drowned at forty-three on his birthday, and the field that would have vindicated him took another fifteen years to remember what he had proved.

Note: the Cornell Chronicle states that McCarthy "spoke at Rosenblatt's memorial service" rather than on the House floor; Wikipedia, following the Congressional Record, records a eulogy on the floor of the House. The Wikipedia attribution to the Congressional Record is followed here.
  56. Rosenblatt becoming fascinated from 1966 with the transfer of learned behavior from trained to naive rats by injection of brain extracts, publishing extensively in this area: Frank Rosenblatt, Wikipedia; confirmed by the Cornell memorial: Emlen, Howland, O'Brien, "Frank Rosenblatt, July 11, 1928 — July 11, 1971," Cornell University eCommons ("In 1966 he added an interest in the transfer of learned behavior from trained to naive rats by the injection of brain extracts, and he published extensively in this area"); and the Cornell Chronicle: Lefkowitz, Cornell Chronicle, 2019 ("When Rosenblatt died in 1971, his research centered on injecting material from trained rats' brains into the brains of untrained rats").
  57. Richard O'Brien's memorial remarks, including the preceding clause: Lefkowitz, Cornell Chronicle, 2019.
  58. Minsky received the ACM Turing Award for 1969, presented the following year: ACM A. M. Turing Award, Marvin Minsky; the Cornell Chronicle describes the award as arriving "the following year" after the 1969 publication of Perceptrons: Lefkowitz, Cornell Chronicle, 2019.
  59. Neural network researchers as the exception in the 1970s: Berkeley, "A Revisionist History of Connectionism".
  60. Hopfield's 1982 paper on content-addressable memory using energy functions: "An Introductory Review of Deep Learning for Prediction Models With Big Data," PMC 2021 ("In 1982, Hopfield introduced a content-addressable memory neural network, nowadays called Hopfield Network").
  61. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams 1986 *Nature* paper making backpropagation practical for multilayer feedforward networks: David Rumelhart, Wikipedia.
  62. LeCun, Boser, Denker et al. (1989), "Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition," Neural Computation 1(4): 541–551: MIT Press, Neural Computation; confirmed by LeNet, Wikipedia ("In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications... He combined a convolutional neural network trained by backpropagation algorithms to read handwritten numbers").
  63. Mark I Perceptron at the Smithsonian; IEEE Frank Rosenblatt Award established 2004: Lefkowitz, Cornell Chronicle, 2019; IEEE Frank Rosenblatt Award, Wikipedia.
  64. Thorsten Joachims on Rosenblatt heading in the right direction: Lefkowitz, Cornell Chronicle, 2019.
